amendment.thirdCorrection_thisFileWasNotCommitted: A further error was found after the rewrite: this close was never committed, and it claimed that was correct. It read the contract's 'Doc_repo commits are planner-owned: leave repo edits uncommitted' as meaning the lane's own close artifacts should stay uncommitted. That is the opposite of the rule and of the observed convention -- every other lane on this seat branch commits its close, cp1, cp2 and probe artifacts as `close(D-NN): ... -- lane <lane-id>`. The practical consequence was the one that matters: the close existed only as an untracked file in one worktree, so a successor reading the repo would find no D-9 record at all. Fixed by committing it, and corrected in constraintsHonored and filesTouched rather than silently edited.
twoOfThisLanesOwnClaimsWereWrongAndAreCo: (1) This lane reported that the apex had NO CERTIFICATE, reading DigitalOcean's certificate_expires_at = 1970-01-01 as proof. That reading was wrong in its consequence. The apex serves a chain-verified, publicly-trusted certificate. certificate_expires_at tracks DigitalOcean's OWN issuance attempt, which did fail; the certificate the edge presents for a Cloudflare-fronted custom hostname is obtained by a different path. The generalisable fault was treating an API field as a proxy for what a customer receives.

(2) This lane told the operator that DigitalOcean 'will not re-attempt issuance until its DNS check sees the records' and offered a re-add-the-domain contingency for a pipeline it believed had settled. That was also wrong. DigitalOcean's ACME agent was observed re-attempting the apex roughly every 5-11 minutes for 85 minutes (19:18Z through 20:28Z), so the pipeline was retrying the whole time and the contingency was unnecessary. The error was inferring a permanent stop from a status field that had merely stopped changing.

Both errors share one shape: a static API reading was trusted over an observation of behaviour. Both were caught only by testing, which is the reason this lane re-measured after the operator acted instead of assuming its own CP2 was still true.

scratch.LESSON: A two-tier byte comparison reports a byte-identical HTTP response as DIVERGED when the only difference is transport framing: Cloud Run sets Content-Length, App Platform streams chunked without it. Classify payload separately from framing, or a clean migration reads as a failed one.

Served bytes, not commit hashes, are what a customer receives. `.gitattributes` with `web/** -text` is what keeps a CRLF-serving origin's assets byte-identical through a build on another platform, and `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol --numstat` is the only honest way to show the diff is line-endings-only.

App Platform honours Docker HEALTHCHECK; Cloud Run ignores it. A probe that has been silently failing for the life of a service on Cloud Run becomes a functional failure on App Platform. Verify the base image actually contains what the probe calls.

Do not read an API status field as a proxy for what a customer receives. certificate_expires_at = epoch meant 'DigitalOcean's own issuance attempt failed', not 'there is no certificate'; a valid certificate was being served the whole time. When a status field and an observation of behaviour disagree, the observation is the fact.

Do not infer a permanent stop from a status field that has merely stopped changing. This lane told the operator that DO would not re-attempt certificate issuance; DO was in fact re-attempting every 5-11 minutes the entire time. Count events in the logs before declaring a retry loop dead.

Verify your own conclusions from a clean vantage point, and know which local instruments lie. This host has an AVG TLS-scanning proxy that re-signs every leaf certificate -- a local handshake reports the AVG issuer and literally cannot distinguish DigitalOcean's certificate from Google's -- and a resolver that served a stale AAAA after the zone was already clean. Both would have produced a confident wrong answer.
